```{r setup}
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(survival)
library(survRM2)
library(metafor)
library(ggplot2)

source("R/hta_methods.R")

trt_levels <- c("Placebo", "Xanomeline Low Dose", "Xanomeline High Dose")
# Okabe-Ito, as in programs/92_figures.R
trt_colours <- c("Placebo" = "#0072B2", "Xanomeline Low Dose" = "#E69F00",
                 "Xanomeline High Dose" = "#D55E00")

fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
fmt_ci <- function(est, lo, hi, d = 2) {
  f <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "NE", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
  paste0(f(est), " (", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), ")")
}

# SAS transport stores missing character values as "".
read_adam <- function(name) {
  read_xpt(file.path("data/adam", paste0(name, ".xpt"))) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, "")))
}
adsl     <- read_adam("adsl")
adae     <- read_adam("adae")
adtte    <- read_adam("adtte")
adqsadas <- read_adam("adqsadas")

# Baseline ADAS-Cog(11) total, the baseline severity variable.
base_adas <- adqsadas %>%
  filter(PARAMCD == "ACTOT", ABLFL == "Y") %>%
  distinct(USUBJID, BASE)

tte <- adtte %>%
  filter(PARAMCD == "TTDE", SAFFL == "Y") %>%
  left_join(base_adas, by = "USUBJID") %>%
  mutate(
    TRTA   = factor(TRTA, levels = trt_levels),
    EVENT  = 1 - CNSR,
    AGEGR1 = factor(AGEGR1, levels = c("<65", "65-80", ">80")),
    SEX    = factor(SEX, levels = c("F", "M")),
    BASEGR = factor(ifelse(BASE <= 21, "<= 21", "> 21"), levels = c("<= 21", "> 21"))
  )
stopifnot(nrow(tte) == 254, !anyNA(tte$BASEGR))
```

## The question and the data

The endpoint is the time from first dose to the first treatment-emergent
dermatologic adverse event. ADTTE already holds it as `PARAMCD = "TTDE"`.
Patients without such an event are censored at the end of their study
participation. The population is the safety population. Patients are
analysed by the treatment they actually received.

This is a harm endpoint. A hazard ratio above 1 means more events on
xanomeline. The xanomeline arms lost many patients early, so the arms were
observed for very different lengths of time. That is the main reason an HTA
body wants adverse events analysed as time to event. A simple proportion
ignores how long each patient was at risk.

```{r counts}
tte %>%
  group_by(Arm = TRTA) %>%
  summarise(N = n(), Events = sum(EVENT), Censored = sum(CNSR),
            `Median observed time, days` = median(AVAL),
            `Longest observed time, days` = max(AVAL))
```

## Kaplan-Meier curves, medians and the log-rank test

The Kaplan-Meier estimate multiplies, over each event time, the share of
patients at risk who did not have the event. Censored patients count as at
risk until they leave. The median is the first time the curve reaches 50%.
Its confidence interval uses the log-log transformation, as in Table 3 of
this repository.

```{r km}
km <- survfit(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA, data = tte, conf.type = "log-log")
kmt <- summary(km)$table

data.frame(
  Arm = trt_levels,
  N = kmt[, "records"],
  Events = kmt[, "events"],
  `Median, days (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(kmt[, "median"], kmt[, "0.95LCL"], kmt[, "0.95UCL"], d = 0),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)
```

Fewer than half of the placebo patients had an event, so the placebo curve
never reaches 50%. Its median is not estimable (NE).

```{r km-plot, fig.height = 5.5}
km_dat <- broom::tidy(km) %>%
  mutate(TRTA = factor(sub("^TRTA=", "", strata), levels = trt_levels)) %>%
  select(TRTA, time, estimate, n.censor)
km_dat <- bind_rows(
  tibble(TRTA = factor(trt_levels, levels = trt_levels), time = 0, estimate = 1, n.censor = 0),
  km_dat
)
risk_times <- seq(0, 196, by = 28)
at_risk <- summary(km, times = risk_times, extend = TRUE)
risk_dat <- tibble(
  TRTA   = factor(sub("^TRTA=", "", at_risk$strata), levels = trt_levels),
  time   = at_risk$time,
  n.risk = at_risk$n.risk
)

p_km <- ggplot(km_dat, aes(time, estimate, colour = TRTA)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = filter(km_dat, n.censor > 0), shape = 3, size = 1.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = trt_colours, breaks = trt_levels) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = risk_times, limits = c(0, 200)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Days since first dose", y = "Free of dermatologic AE",
       colour = NULL, caption = "+ = censored. Dotted line: median.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey40"))

p_risk <- ggplot(risk_dat, aes(time, TRTA, label = n.risk, colour = TRTA)) +
  geom_text(size = 3.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = trt_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = risk_times, limits = c(0, 200)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(trt_levels)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Number at risk") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 10))

cowplot::plot_grid(p_km, p_risk, ncol = 1, rel_heights = c(4, 1.3), align = "v", axis = "lr")
```

The log-rank test compares, at every event time, the observed number of
events in one arm with the number expected if both arms had the same hazard.
It sums the differences over time and divides by their variance. The result
is a chi-squared statistic with one degree of freedom for two arms.

The code below does this by hand for each active arm against placebo. It
then calls `survival::survdiff()`. The two must agree.

```{r logrank}
vs_placebo_data <- function(arm) {
  tte %>% filter(TRTA %in% c("Placebo", arm)) %>% droplevels()
}

lr_tab <- lapply(trt_levels[-1], function(arm) {
  d    <- vs_placebo_data(arm)
  hand <- logrank_hand(d$AVAL, d$EVENT, d$TRTA == arm)
  pkg  <- survdiff(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA, data = d)
  data.frame(Comparison = paste(arm, "vs placebo"),
             `O - E (active)` = round(hand$o_minus_e, 2),
             `Chi-squared, hand` = hand$chisq,
             `Chi-squared, survdiff` = pkg$chisq,
             `p-value` = fmt_p(hand$p), check.names = FALSE)
})
bind_rows(lr_tab)

# Three-arm test, for completeness.
lr3 <- survdiff(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA, data = tte)
```

The three-arm log-rank test gives chi-squared `r round(lr3$chisq, 1)` on 2
degrees of freedom (p `r fmt_p(pchisq(lr3$chisq, 2, lower.tail = FALSE))`).

## Cox model: hazard ratio against placebo

The Cox model assumes that the hazard in the active arm is a constant
multiple of the hazard in the placebo arm. That multiple is the hazard ratio.
The model leaves the shape of the baseline hazard free.

The stratified model gives each pooled site (`SITEGR1`) its own baseline
hazard and estimates one common hazard ratio across sites. The factor was
fixed before the analysis. It is the same factor that the primary efficacy
ANCOVA adjusts for. Stratification is used for three reasons. Sites can
differ in how often and how carefully skin events are recorded. Stratifying
removes that difference from the comparison without assuming how it acts on
the hazard. It also keeps the analysis close to the design of the trial,
which is what HTA bodies expect.

```{r cox}
cox_tab <- lapply(trt_levels[-1], function(arm) {
  d  <- vs_placebo_data(arm)
  c0 <- summary(coxph(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA, data = d))$conf.int
  c1 <- summary(coxph(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA + strata(SITEGR1), data = d))$conf.int
  data.frame(Comparison = paste(arm, "vs placebo"),
             `HR (95% CI), unstratified` = fmt_ci(c0[1, 1], c0[1, 3], c0[1, 4]),
             `HR (95% CI), stratified by SITEGR1` = fmt_ci(c1[1, 1], c1[1, 3], c1[1, 4]),
             check.names = FALSE)
})
bind_rows(cox_tab)
```

Both doses raise the hazard of a first dermatologic event about four- to
fivefold. Stratification barely moves the estimates. That is expected in a
randomised trial where arms are balanced within sites.

## Checking proportional hazards

The hazard ratio is one number for the whole follow-up. It is only a fair
summary if the ratio is roughly constant over time. Three checks are used.

1. **Schoenfeld residuals.** For each event, the residual compares the
   treatment of the patient who had the event with the average treatment of
   those at risk. If the hazard ratio is constant, the residuals show no trend
   over time. `cox.zph()` tests the correlation between the scaled residuals
   and time.
2. **Plot of the scaled residuals over time.** The smooth line is an
   estimate of the log hazard ratio at each time. A flat line supports
   proportional hazards.
3. **Log-log plot.** Under proportional hazards, the curves of
   log(-log S(t)) against log(t) are parallel. Crossing or converging curves
   are a warning.

```{r ph}
cox_all <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA, data = tte)
zph <- cox.zph(cox_all, transform = "km", terms = FALSE)  # one row per arm
zph
```

```{r ph-plot, fig.height = 4}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(zph[1], resid = TRUE, se = TRUE, main = "Low dose vs placebo", ylab = "Beta(t)")
abline(h = coef(cox_all)[1], lty = 2, col = "grey40")
plot(zph[2], resid = TRUE, se = TRUE, main = "High dose vs placebo", ylab = "Beta(t)")
abline(h = coef(cox_all)[2], lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

```{r loglog, fig.height = 4}
broom::tidy(km) %>%
  filter(estimate > 0, estimate < 1) %>%
  mutate(TRTA = factor(sub("^TRTA=", "", strata), levels = trt_levels)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(log(time), log(-log(estimate)), colour = TRTA)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = trt_colours) +
  labs(x = "log(days)", y = "log(-log S(t))", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The global test gives p = `r sprintf("%.2f", zph$table["GLOBAL", "p"])`.
The residual plots are flat within their bands, and the log-log curves run
roughly parallel. There is no evidence against proportional hazards here.

**If the check had failed**, a single hazard ratio would be an average of a
changing effect. Its value would then depend on how long patients were
followed and on when they were censored. I would then:

- report the restricted mean survival time difference (next section), which
  needs no proportional-hazards assumption,
- report a piecewise hazard ratio with time intervals fixed in advance, by
  splitting follow-up with `survSplit()` and fitting a treatment-by-interval
  interaction,
- report event-free proportions at fixed time points (milestones) with their
  differences,
- for testing, consider a weighted or max-combo log-rank test fixed in the
  analysis plan.

## Restricted mean survival time

The restricted mean survival time (RMST) up to a horizon τ is the area under
the Kaplan-Meier curve from 0 to τ. Here it is the mean number of days free
of a dermatologic event during the first τ days. The difference between arms
is in days. It does not need proportional hazards, and patients and
clinicians can read it directly.

τ = 168 days (Week 24, the planned treatment period) was fixed in advance.
It must not exceed the longest observed time in any arm. The shortest of
these is 189 days.
Few xanomeline patients remain at risk near day 168. They no longer have
events, so the curve is flat there and adds little variance.

The code computes the area and its variance by hand, then with
`survRM2::rmst2()`.

```{r rmst}
tau <- 168
rmst_tab <- lapply(trt_levels[-1], function(arm) {
  d    <- vs_placebo_data(arm)
  act  <- d$TRTA == arm
  hand <- rmst_diff_hand(d$AVAL, d$EVENT, act, tau)
  pkg  <- rmst2(d$AVAL, d$EVENT, as.integer(act), tau = tau)$unadjusted.result
  data.frame(Comparison = paste(arm, "vs placebo"),
             `RMST active, days` = round(hand$rmst1, 1),
             `RMST placebo, days` = round(hand$rmst0, 1),
             `Difference (95% CI), hand` = fmt_ci(hand$diff, hand$lower, hand$upper, d = 1),
             `Difference (95% CI), survRM2` = fmt_ci(pkg[1, 1], pkg[1, 2], pkg[1, 3], d = 1),
             check.names = FALSE)
})
bind_rows(rmst_tab)
```

Over the first 24 weeks, high-dose patients were free of dermatologic events
for about 79 fewer days on average than placebo patients.

## Subgroup analyses

Three subgroup variables were fixed in advance: age group (`AGEGR1`), sex,
and baseline disease severity. Severity is the baseline ADAS-Cog(11) total,
split at the pooled median of 21 without looking at the arms. Higher scores
mean worse cognition. The comparison is the high dose against placebo.

For each subgroup level the code fits a Cox model within that level. The
question that matters is different. Does the hazard ratio differ between
levels? The test of treatment-by-subgroup interaction answers it. It is a
likelihood-ratio test comparing a model with treatment and subgroup against
one that adds their interaction.

```{r subgroups}
hd <- vs_placebo_data("Xanomeline High Dose")

subgroup_vars <- c(AGEGR1 = "Age group", SEX = "Sex", BASEGR = "Baseline ADAS-Cog(11)")

sub_res <- lapply(names(subgroup_vars), function(v) {
  f_main <- as.formula(paste("Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA +", v))
  f_int  <- as.formula(paste("Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA *", v))
  p_int  <- anova(coxph(f_main, data = hd), coxph(f_int, data = hd))[2, "Pr(>|Chi|)"]
  lv <- levels(hd[[v]])
  bind_rows(lapply(lv, function(l) {
    d  <- hd[hd[[v]] == l, ]
    ci <- summary(coxph(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA, data = d))$conf.int
    data.frame(Variable = subgroup_vars[[v]], Level = l,
               N = nrow(d),
               `Events (HD / PBO)` = paste0(sum(d$EVENT[d$TRTA != "Placebo"]), " / ",
                                            sum(d$EVENT[d$TRTA == "Placebo"])),
               hr = ci[1, 1], lo = ci[1, 3], hi = ci[1, 4],
               p_int = p_int, check.names = FALSE)
  }))
})
sub_res <- bind_rows(sub_res)
overall <- summary(coxph(Surv(AVAL, EVENT) ~ TRTA, data = hd))$conf.int

sub_res %>%
  mutate(`HR (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(hr, lo, hi),
         `Interaction p` = ifelse(duplicated(Variable), "", fmt_p(p_int))) %>%
  select(Variable, Level, N, `Events (HD / PBO)`, `HR (95% CI)`, `Interaction p`)
```

```{r forest, fig.height = 4.5}
forest_dat <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(Variable = "All patients", Level = "", hr = overall[1, 1],
             lo = overall[1, 3], hi = overall[1, 4], p_int = NA),
  sub_res %>% select(Variable, Level, hr, lo, hi, p_int)
) %>%
  mutate(label = ifelse(Level == "", Variable, paste0(Variable, ": ", Level)),
         label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)))

ggplot(forest_dat, aes(hr, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall[1, 1], linetype = "dashed", colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.2) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = Level == ""), size = 2.5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(15, 18), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio, high dose vs placebo (log scale)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Dashed line: overall hazard ratio. Values above 1 mean more events on xanomeline.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey40"))
```

None of the interaction tests is significant at the 5% level. The smallest
p-value is `r fmt_p(min(sub_res$p_int))`, for
`r tolower(sub_res$Variable[which.min(sub_res$p_int)])`. All subgroup intervals
include the overall estimate.

**Multiplicity.** Three subgroup variables give three interaction tests and
seven subgroup estimates. At the 5% level, one false signal somewhere is
quite likely even when the effect is the same in everyone.

**Why a subgroup p-value alone proves nothing.** A significant effect in one
subgroup and a non-significant effect in another does not show that the
effects differ. The second subgroup may simply be smaller. Only the
interaction test compares the subgroups with each other.

## Binary endpoint: at least one adverse event

The share of patients with at least one treatment-emergent adverse event
(TEAE) is a second, simpler summary. Three effect measures describe the
same 2x2 table, and an HTA dossier usually reports all three.

- **Risk ratio (RR):** risk on active divided by risk on placebo.
- **Odds ratio (OR):** odds on active divided by odds on placebo.
- **Risk difference (RD):** risk on active minus risk on placebo, shown as
  a proportion (0.20 is 20 percentage points).

RR and OR are estimated on the log scale and back-transformed. The code
computes them by hand and with `metafor::escalc()`.

```{r binary}
any_teae <- adsl %>%
  filter(SAFFL == "Y") %>%
  mutate(TRTA = factor(TRT01A, levels = trt_levels),
         ANY  = USUBJID %in% adae$USUBJID[adae$TRTEMFL == "Y"]) %>%
  group_by(TRTA) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(ANY), N = n(), .groups = "drop")

pbo <- any_teae %>% filter(TRTA == "Placebo")

bin_tab <- lapply(trt_levels[-1], function(arm) {
  a    <- any_teae %>% filter(TRTA == arm)
  hand <- effect_2x2_hand(a$n, a$N, pbo$n, pbo$N)
  pkg  <- sapply(c("RR", "OR", "RD"), function(m)
    escalc(m, ai = a$n, n1i = a$N, ci = pbo$n, n2i = pbo$N)$yi)
  data.frame(Comparison = paste(arm, "vs placebo"),
             `Active, n/N (%)` = sprintf("%d/%d (%.1f%%)", a$n, a$N, 100 * a$n / a$N),
             `Placebo, n/N (%)` = sprintf("%d/%d (%.1f%%)", pbo$n, pbo$N, 100 * pbo$n / pbo$N),
             Measure = hand$measure,
             `Estimate (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(hand$estimate, hand$lower, hand$upper),
             `Hand - escalc (analysis scale)` = signif(hand$yi - pkg, 2),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
})
bind_rows(bin_tab)
```

The three measures tell the same story at very different sizes. For the
high dose the risk ratio is about 1.27 and the odds ratio about 7.4. When
the event is common, here over 75% on placebo, the odds ratio is far from
the risk ratio. It should not be read as "seven times the risk". The risk
difference of about 20 percentage points is the easiest to read. It also
lets one compute a number needed to harm of about 5.

## What a German dossier would ask here

In the German benefit assessment (AMNOG), the company submits a dossier and
IQWiG assesses it for the Federal Joint Committee (G-BA). For a safety
endpoint like this one, the dossier would usually be asked for the
following.

- **Adverse events as time to event.** Arms are often observed for different
  lengths of time, for example because patients stop treatment early. A
  proportion then compares unequal windows. A Kaplan-Meier analysis with a
  hazard ratio deals with that.
- **Effect measures with 95% confidence intervals.** Hazard ratios for time
  to event, and relative risks or odds ratios with risk differences for
  binary endpoints. Each with the number of patients and events per arm.
- **Standard sets of adverse events.** All adverse events, serious ones,
  severe ones (for example CTCAE grade 3 or higher) and discontinuations due
  to adverse events. Specific events by system organ class and preferred
  term are added where they matter.
- **Subgroup analyses with interaction tests.** Usually age, sex, region or
  centre and disease severity, fixed in advance. The interaction test, not a
  p-value within one subgroup, decides whether an effect differs. Results
  are shown only for subgroups large enough to support them.
- **Methods fixed before the data are seen**, with sensitivity analyses
  where an assumption such as proportional hazards is in doubt.
